otherStraights.value: 3 straights hold the 12 main rf cavities (sectors 36, 37, 40); 1 holds the superconducting bunch-lengthening cavity (+ longitudinal-feedback kickers); 1 holds injection (pulsed septum + 3 stripline kickers)

otherStraights.note: FDR placed extraction kickers + harmonic cavity in the sector-38 straight and injection (septum, kickers, A:M1 swap-out dump) in sector 39 (fdr2 2-2.8, 2-3.10). As built, injection and extraction use the same 3 kickers in one straight (desy24, ler25 slide 2, srp2024). A May 2024 APS all-hands slide deck (G. Decker) reportedly labels the injection straight as sector 39, but the verifier could not open it (404/DNS failure), so the as-built sector numbers for injection, swap-out dump and BLS remain unconfirmed. IPAC'25 Fig. 2 puts the injection point at s = 1104 m, i.e. at the end/start of the lattice.

magnetStrength.value: quadrupoles up to ~80-100 T/m (Q7 86 T/m, Q1 79 T/m), sextupoles up to ~5,000-6,800 T/m^2; vanadium-permendur pole tips; 13 mm minimum pole-tip radius
magnetStrength.source: fdr2 Tables 2.5-2.6 and 2-3.1; ipac21 ('order 100 T/m and 6800 T/m^2', 13-14 mm bores); apsNSR: magnets 'up to five times stronger' than the originals

longitudinalGradientDipoles.value: M1 and M2 each made of 5 field steps (e.g. M1 0.65 T -> 0.14 T); all M1s in series on one supply, all M2s on another

reverseBends.value: Q4, Q5, Q8 are quadrupoles mounted off-axis so the beam also sees a weak dipole field bending the 'wrong' way (-0.07 to -0.31 deg each). The extra dipole 'knob' lets the designers shape the dispersion independently of the beta functions, lowering the natural emittance from 67 pm (same lattice without reverse bends) to 42 pm
reverseBends.source: fdr2 2-2.1 ('allowing reduction of the natural emittance to 42 pm compared to 67 pm in the design without reverse bends'; 'help manipulate the dispersion independently of the beta functions'), Table 2.4
reverseBends.note: fdr2 2-2.1.3: the weak dipole fields of Q4 and Q5 sit where the dispersion is large, so they are very effective at adjusting the damping partition and let the dispersion be raised in the sextupoles and brought back down in M2; without reverse bending there the minimum emittance would be 58 pm. Angles from fdr2 Table 2.4: Q4 -0.098 deg, Q5 -0.066 deg, Q8 -0.307 deg (verified).

totalBendingAngle.source: derived from fdr2 Table 2.4: +9.945 deg - 0.942 deg per sector x 40; ipac21 quotes 'from 360 to 435 degrees'

emittanceScaling.value: epsilon ~ E^2 / (N_sectors^3 x N_dipoles^3): going from 2 to 7 dipoles per sector alone gives ~40x reduction

phaseAdvance.value: 3 pi (x), pi (y) between the two dispersion bumps of each sector, cancelling sextupole geometric effects

insertionDevices.name: Planar hybrid permanent-magnet undulator (HPMU)
insertionDevices.what: Two rows of NdFeB magnets with vanadium-permendur poles above and below a thin aluminium vacuum chamber; the gap between the rows sets the field and so the x-ray energy.

periods_cm.source: ipac24und Table 1 (5 new period lengths in 46 magnetic structures; 26 existing structures with 4 period lengths reused)

parametersAtMinGap.source: ipac24und Table 1 (E1 = first-harmonic energy at 6.0 GeV, min gap)
parametersAtMinGap.note: Higher harmonics (3rd, 5th, ... up to ~13th) reach tens to >100 keV.

length.value: ~2.4 m (full) or ~2.1 m (canted); up to 4.8 m of undulator per straight
length.note: Derived check from idsector2026 (N x period): in-line devices 2.35-2.38 m of magnet (e.g. 112 x 2.1 cm, 84 x 2.8 cm, 72 x 3.3 cm, 175 x 1.35 cm); canted devices 2.05-2.07 m (98 x 2.1 cm, 74 x 2.8 cm, 62 x 3.3 cm, 153 x 1.35 cm).

minimumGap.value: 8.5 mm for periods <= 2.8 cm, 9.0 mm for 3.0 cm, 10 mm for >= 3.3 cm (design device minimum)
minimumGap.source: idsector2026 note 7; fdr3 Table 3.22 (8.2 mm absolute limit)

gapControl.value: 0.5 um resolution, < 3 um repeatability, 1 mm/s, max gap 125-180 mm

photonEnergyControl.value: ~1 eV while scanning at 1 keV/s (new modular ID control system, up to 13 axes)

phaseError.value: requirement <= 3 deg rms, achieved <= 2.5 deg (typ.); 2.37 deg for a full sector of two in-phase 2.5-cm IDs

magnetMaterial.value: NdFeB with grain-boundary-diffused heavy rare earths (HcJ >= 21 kOe, >= 28 kOe within 3 mm of surface) against radiation demagnetisation; vanadium-permendur poles

phaseShifters.unit: phase shifters (with correctors) between in-line pairs

power.value: about 1-10 kW total, 100-230 kW/mrad^2 on axis per device at 200 mA (device dependent)

frontEndLimit.value: high-heat-load front end: 21 kW total, 590 kW/mrad^2

insertionDevices.name: Revolver undulator
insertionDevices.what: Two different magnet structures mounted at 90 deg on one strongback; with the gap open the assembly rotates to pick the period (e.g. 2.1 cm or 2.5 cm), giving the beamline two tuning ranges in one device.

insertionDevices.name: Canted undulator pair
insertionDevices.what: Two ~2.1-m undulators in one straight with small electromagnets that steer the electron beam by 0.5 / 1.0 / 0.5 mrad, so the two x-ray beams leave 1 mrad apart and feed two independent beamlines.

geometry.value: 0.5 mrad upstream, 1.0 mrad centre (with corrector), 0.5 mrad downstream; magnet lengths 2,072 mm each; device centres -1229.5 mm / +1234.5 mm from the sector centreline

insertionDevices.name: Planar superconducting undulator (SCU)
insertionDevices.what: NbTi wire wound in grooves of two iron cores and cooled to 4.2 K; superconducting coils give a stronger field than permanent magnets at the same period and gap, which is best for very hard x-rays (>~50-60 keV).

plannedScope.source: sp2025; fdr3 Table 3.24 (eight devices in four 4.8-m cryostats)
plannedScope.note: fdr3 Table 3.24 gives a 1.2-m magnetic length for the 18.5-mm canted pair at sector 28; sp2025 says 1.3 m. The FDR also planned a 1.8-cm SCU downstream at 6-ID (fdr3 Table 3.13) that is not among the eight new SCUs; sector 6 now has two canted HPMUs (2.3 and 2.7 cm).

cryostat.value: 4.8-m-long cryostat, magnets at 4.2 K cooled by five 2-W 4-K cryocoolers; beam chamber < 20 K on a separate cryocooler

gap.value: 8.0 mm magnetic gap, 6.3 mm beam-chamber aperture

K.value: Kmax ~1.63 (16.5 mm, HEXM design); Ky 2.291 (18.5 mm, CHEX design, E1 5.1 keV)
K.source: fdr4 Table 4.27 and CHEX source table

status.value: NOT INSTALLED as of 2026-09-22. Cryostats delivered and cores trained, but long, short-period cores showed reliability problems ('magnet failures and fabrication delays', ipac25scu); a new core design was developed. Plan (Feb. 2025): first pair at sector 11 end-2025, remaining 6 devices 2026-2027; first in-line SCU 'scheduled for installation in May 2026' (sp2025). The Sep. 22, 2026 ID table still lists interim permanent-magnet undulators in sectors 1, 11, 20 and 28, so both dates have slipped.
status.source: sp2025; ipac25scu; idsector2026; ipac24und ('SCUs are planned to be installed later')
status.note: The older 1.6-cm SCU (21 periods) operated in the pre-upgrade ring (idring2016).

insertionDevices.name: SCAPE - SuperConducting Arbitrarily Polarizing Emitter
insertionDevices.what: Four superconducting magnet arrays (top, bottom, left, right) around a small round beam pipe, with the side pair shifted a quarter period; changing the currents gives horizontal, vertical, elliptical or circular polarization. Only possible because on-axis swap-out injection allows tiny round ID chambers.

design.value: 2 x 1.3 m, 35 mm period (conservative; 30 mm and up to 1.8 m possible), for POLAR (4-ID), L-H/L-V/circular up to 27 keV

chamber.value: round beam pipe with only 6 mm inside diameter (the main injection-loss point in simulations)

prototype.value: 0.5 m long, 30 mm period, 16.5 periods, 10 mm magnetic gap, NbTi, 540 A operating current; planar and circular modes demonstrated in a liquid-helium bath

status.value: Post-project scope, not installed (Sep. 2026 table lists two 3.0-cm HPMUs at sector 4)

insertionDevices.name: IEX quasi-periodic electromagnetic undulator (sector 29)
insertionDevices.what: 12.5-cm-period electromagnet that can produce circular, horizontal-linear or vertical-linear polarization for intermediate-energy (soft) x-rays; reused unchanged with a new vacuum chamber.

parameters.value: 12.5 cm period, 38 periods; first-harmonic energy at 6 GeV: 0.32 keV circular (Kx = Ky = 2.73), 0.18 keV horizontal-linear (Ky = 5.39), 0.32 keV vertical-linear (Kx = 3.86)
parameters.source: idsector2026 (S29 row and note 9: Ix=34.4 A, Iy=20.7 A circular; Iy=47.6 A horizontal linear; Ix=50.3 A vertical linear); ipac24und
parameters.note: Corrected by verifier: the earlier text assigned 0.18 keV to vertical-linear; the Sep. 2026 table gives 0.18 keV for HORIZONTAL-linear mode (the strong vertical field Ky = 5.39 makes the electrons oscillate horizontally).

insertionDevices.name: Insertion-device vacuum chamber (IDVC)
insertionDevices.what: The thin aluminium tube the electrons travel through inside an undulator; the magnets sit outside it (out-of-vacuum undulators).

parameters.value: 6063-T5 aluminium extrusion, 6.3 mm (h) x 16 mm (w) elliptical aperture, 0.6 mm wall, ~5 m long (5.363 m flange to flange), NEG cartridges + ion pump + photon absorber; thin-nose height within +/-75 um

count.value: 35 ID front ends - all original ID front ends replaced by new high-heat-load or canted-undulator front ends; the existing bending-magnet front ends (23 installed in 2019, 20 with operating beamlines) reused with minor modifications
count.source: fdr3 3-1 ('will require all the original ID front ends to be replaced'; 'there are 23 BM front ends installed, of which only 20 beamlines are in operation'; 'The current BM front ends will undergo minor modifications and will be reused')

types.value: High-Heat-Load FE (two in-line undulators; limits 21 kW, 590 kW/mrad^2), Canted-Undulator FE (two beams 1 mrad apart), Bending-Magnet FE

features.value: permanent-magnet 'clearing magnet' to dump any stray electrons during swap-out; GRID x-ray BPMs for long-term beam stability; 2 x 2 mm exit mask (two apertures for canted); window or windowless (differential pump) exit
features.note: The permanent-magnet clearing magnet sits in the extraction port just upstream of the safety shutter so that electrons mis-steered during a swap-out failure are bent into shielding (fdr3 3-2.1) - a new requirement for APS-U.

xbpmRequirement.value: XBPM1 resolution 12 um (H) / 10 um (V) over 7 days; AC 3.7 / 2.4 um

concept.value: On-axis 'swap-out' injection: instead of topping up stored bunches (accumulation), the weakest stored bunch is kicked out to a dump and replaced in the same rf bucket by a fresh, full-charge bunch from the injector - no accumulation needed, so the ring can work with a tiny dynamic aperture (~+/-1.5 mm).

worldFirst.value: APS-U is the first storage-ring light source to use (multi-bunch) swap-out injection; first multi-bunch swap-out on 2024-04-29 (12 bunches, 1.1 mA target, 30-s interval, 0.6 nC from the BTS)

plane.source: desy24; ler25; ipac21 ('injected horizontally on-axis using a pulsed 1.4-T septum magnet, 3 horizontal fast kickers')
plane.note: The 2019 FDR described vertical injection with a DC Lambertson septum and separate extraction kickers in the sector-38 straight (fdr2 2-2.8, 2-3.6). By 2021 the design had changed to horizontal injection with a pulsed septum; as built, the same three kickers inject the new bunch and kick the old one out (desy24, ler25, srp2024).

septum.value: pulsed, single-turn, direct-drive septum magnet: 1.42 T peak over 1.493 m, blade tapering to 3 mm; 18 kA in a 1-mm copper bus
septum.source: napac25 ('a septum blade that tapers to 3 mm thickness at the downstream end'; 23 days, ~1 million pulses); ipac25; ler25 slides 26-27
septum.note: First septum failed after ~1 million pulses (23 days); the spare then leaked; the repaired original went back in. Its stored-beam tube was bowed so that it touched the design orbit ~0.7 m from the exit, so the magnet was pivoted about its exit (0.7 mrad per napac25/ipac25; 1.5 mrad per ler25 slide 27). The septum chamber was replaced by Oct. 2025 (ler25 slide 21) and a new septum design is being built (ler25 slide 27).

injectionKickers.value: 3 stripline kickers in one straight, horizontal, 3 mrad total, ~11 ns pulses (+/-~25 kV, 'about 27 kV' pulsers); allow filling every third rf bucket
injectionKickers.source: ler25 slide 5; desy24 slide 12; ipac21; harkay23; srp2024
injectionKickers.note: A 2024 APS all-hands slide reportedly lists 27-kV stripline pulsers with a 20-ns pulse (search-engine summary only, not opened); ler25 slide 5 and ipac21 give ~11-ns pulses. Treat 11 ns as the as-built kicker pulse length per the 2025 commissioning slides.

gapSeptumToKicker.unit: mm (horizontal gap between septum wall and first kicker blade)

emittanceExchange.value: 6 skew quadrupoles in the BTS swap the booster beam's large horizontal and small vertical emittances so it fits the 2.8-mm gap

decoherenceKicker.value: vertical, 0.2 mrad, 11 ns, fired 200-250 turns before injection to blow up the outgoing bunch and protect the swap-out dump (~100x lower particle density in design)
decoherenceKicker.source: ler25 slide 5 (200 turns); desy24 and napac25 (250 turns); fdr2 2-2.8.2
decoherenceKicker.note: The FDR (2-2.9) describes the same pre-kick idea for the superseded vertical scheme: a weak stripline 'pre-kicker' ~250 turns ahead reduces the energy density on the dump by two orders of magnitude.

fanOutKicker.value: vertical, 0.1 mrad, 5 us half-sine over a full turn; fires on a whole-beam abort to spread all bunches over the beam-dump surface

program.value: fills the requested pattern at 1 Hz, then swaps out the weakest bunch at the requested interval

replacementCriterion.value: design: a bunch is replaced when its charge has fallen to about 90% of nominal; in 2025 operation the weakest bunch is replaced on a fixed ~20-s clock, allowing larger drops (see sampleParameters216)

intervalDesign.value: about 25-30 s (48 bunches, 3.5-4 h lifetime) and 7.5-18 s (324 bunches)
intervalDesign.source: ipac21; fdr2 Table 2.13 (16-30 s round beam, 8-10 s flat 324-bunch)

intervalOperational.value: kept close to 20 s (200 mA, 216 bunches, Oct. 2025)
intervalOperational.source: ler25 slide 23 ('Keeping swap-out interval close to 20 seconds')
intervalOperational.note: With a ~2-h lifetime this means each bunch drops by roughly 40-50% before it is replaced, far more than the 10% assumed in the FDR; the resulting bunch-to-bunch charge non-uniformity is accepted.

sampleParameters216.source: ler25 slide 23 ('Sample swap-out parameters for 200 mA and 216 bunches'); column order (Drop % | BTS charge nC | Interval s) confirmed by verifier from the rendered slide image.

initialFill.value: each bunch first filled with slightly more than I_total/N_bunches = 3.4 nC (216 bunches)

injectionEfficiency.value: very good despite septum aperture limit; shot-to-shot variation < 1% rms over 2 months of user operation

electronsInjected.value: ~40x more electrons injected than with top-up at the old APS; ~90% of them end in the shielded swap-out dump
electronsInjected.note: Both numbers are FDR design values that assume bunches are replaced at ~90% of their charge. In 2025 operation bunches drop by ~40-50% before replacement (ler25 slide 23), so roughly half of the injected charge, not 90%, ends in the swap-out dump (derived by verifier).

injectorChargeNeeded.value: 17 nC (48 bunches) ... 2.5 nC (324 bunches) per shot at 200 mA

swapOut.figureNote: FDR Figs. 2.17-2.18 show the superseded 2019 vertical-injection layout; use them only as background.

dumpsAndCollimators.value: Design (FDR 2019): five horizontal whole-beam dumps/collimators (aluminium, nominal +/-4.8-mm aperture, just upstream of A:Q4 where horizontal beta and dispersion are largest) in sectors 37, 38, 39, 40 and 1, inside the thicker 'Zone F' tunnel shielding; their surfaces can be moved vertically to present a fresh surface after a dump, because a full 200-mA beam dumped in one spot 'will carve a groove in any kind of material'. A whole-beam dump is triggered by tripping the rf. The swap-out dump was a +/-4.58-mm vertical collimator inside the A:M1 magnet of sector 39 (vertical-injection design). As built (2025): collimators sit ~3 mm from the orbit rather than the expected ~4.5 mm, prioritising ID protection over lifetime; the fan-out kicker spreads the bunches over the dump surface during a full-beam abort.
dumpsAndCollimators.note: Added by verifier. The as-built location of the swap-out dump after the change to horizontal injection is not given in any source opened.

purpose.value: Passive 'bunch-lengthening system' (BLS): stretches each electron bunch so electrons collide less often inside the bunch (Touschek scattering), raising lifetime; also eases intrabeam scattering and rf heating of chamber parts

type.value: single-cell superconducting niobium cavity, TESLA cell shape, beam-driven (no external rf drive)

frequency.unit: MHz (4th harmonic of the 352-MHz main rf)
frequency.note: ipac24bls quotes the tuning reference as '1296 x beam revolution frequency or 1.408321 GHz'; 4 x 352.056 MHz (fdr2 Table 2.48) = 1408.22 MHz, so the last digits of that quote are inconsistent (likely a typo).

temperature.unit: K (superfluid helium via J-T valve inside the cryomodule)

cryomodule.value: 2-m cryomodule; with HOM absorbers and tapers occupies 2.4 m (just under half a ~5-m straight); the other half holds longitudinal-feedback kickers

value.tuner: pneumatic helium-bellows tuner (ATLAS heritage), ~600 kHz range

parameters.source: ipac24bls Table 1 and text (nominal values, 'final values TBD')

cryoPlant.value: dedicated Linde LR140 helium refrigerator, up to 2.5 g/s of 4.3-K liquid helium

lifetimeGain.value: about 2x measured (4x expected); lifetime 1.5 h at zero BLS voltage (100 mA, 162 bunches)

measuredProfile.value: double-peaked (over-stretched) bunch profile, peak ratio ~1.6:1, as predicted

history.value: installed before commissioning; tested at 0.5 MV with 50 mA (June 2024); first use with user beam Oct. 8 (2024, year inferred) at 0.5 MV after quench-interlock issues; 1.1 MV at 200 mA by 2025
history.source: desy24 slide 18; ler25 slide 18; sp2025 ('already operating')

designLifetimeTarget.value: ~3.5 h (48 bunches, 200 mA) vs ~1 h without the BLS

brightness.definition: Brightness (also 'brilliance') = photons per second per mm^2 of source area per mrad^2 of beam divergence in a 0.1% energy bandwidth. It measures how many photons come from how small a spot into how narrow a cone - what you need to focus x-rays to tiny spots or to do coherent experiments.

statements.text: The upgraded APS produces X-ray beams 'up to 500 times brighter' than the original APS.
statements.note: Facility headline number; the gain depends on photon energy and on which undulator is compared.

statements.text: At 20 keV, with an undulator optimized for 20 keV, brightness and coherent flux rise by a factor of about 540 (brightness mode 3.25e22 vs 6e19 ph/s/mm^2/mrad^2/0.1%BW).

Over a broad range of hard X-ray energies up to and beyond 100 keV the design gain is a factor of 100 to 1000; the project goal was at least two orders of magnitude for >20 keV, 10-100x more single-bunch brightness for timing experiments, and twice the average flux.
statements.source: fdr2 2-1.2; fdr1 1-2; ipac21 ('two to three orders of magnitude in the 10-100 keV range'; 'twice the spectral flux')

statements.text: The gain depends on photon energy: in the IPAC'21 design envelope it is roughly x200 at 10 keV, x700 at 20 keV and x600-800 at 50-100 keV for brightness, and roughly x160 at 10 keV and x600 at 20 keV for coherent flux.
statements.source: derived from digitized ipac21 Fig. 1 (see dataPoints, +/- ~20%)
statements.note: Reason: the old horizontal emittance (3.1 nm) was far above the photon 'diffraction limit' lambda/4pi at all hard-X-ray energies, so shrinking it helps most where lambda/4pi is smallest (high energy).

statements.text: Horizontal electron emittance fell from ~3,100 pm to ~42 pm (natural; 28-44 pm measured depending on coupling) - a factor of ~75, which APS rounds to 'almost a factor of 100'.
statements.source: sp2025 ('lowered by almost a factor of 100 to 40 pm.rad'); fdr2 Table 2.1; ipac25 Table 1

statements.text: World-record low emittance for a synchrotron light source at the time: 45 pm (flat beam, 50 mA) and 28 pm (round beam), vs 134 pm previous record at ESRF-EBS.
statements.note: 33 pm measured at 200 mA in April 2025 (upd202504). 'World record' refers to Aug. 2024. Check by verifier: China's HEPS (also 6 GeV, design ~35 pm) reported a measured 93 pm in January 2025 (ihep2025), so no lower measured emittance than APS-U's was found as of Oct. 2026.

statements.text: More than 100-fold increase in coherent flux; 'over two orders of magnitude' increase in brightness and coherence.
Superconducting undulators, once installed, are expected to add about another factor 3 in brightness above 50 keV; the objective KPP brightness is expected to be exceeded 3-4x with in-line SCUs.
Approximate transverse coherent fraction (zero current, no energy spread, 2.4-m undulator): at 10 keV ~0.05% for the old APS vs ~3% (round) to ~6% (flat) for APS-U; at 20 keV ~0.015% vs ~1-3%.
statements.source: derived (formula in dataPoints 'coherentFractionEstimate'); consistent with beamline design values 4.2-5.6% at 10 keV and 0.5-0.9% at 25 keV (fdr4 Tables 4.41, 4.51)

statements.text: APS-U horizontal emittance is comparable to the photon emittance lambda/4pi at ~2-3.5 keV (42-29 pm); the flat-beam vertical emittance (~4 pm) matches lambda/4pi at ~25 keV. The old ring's 3.1 nm matched lambda/4pi only at ~30 eV.
No measured APS-U brightness curve has been published that we could find; all curves below are design calculations.
statements.source: search of APS news, JACoW 2024-2026, sp2025 (brightness KPP measurement was planned after SCU installation)

exhibitNumbers.label: Speed of the electrons
exhibitNumbers.value: 99.9999996% of the speed of light - only ~1.1 m/s slower than light
exhibitNumbers.explanation: At 6 GeV the Lorentz factor is gamma = 6000/0.511 = 11,742, so 1 - v/c = 1/(2 gamma^2) = 3.6e-9, i.e. c - v = 1.09 m/s (a brisk walk).

exhibitNumbers.label: Laps per second
exhibitNumbers.value: 271,647 times around the 1.1-km ring every second
exhibitNumbers.explanation: Revolution frequency f0 = c / C = 299,792,458 / 1103.609 m.

exhibitNumbers.label: One lap
exhibitNumbers.value: 3.68 microseconds

exhibitNumbers.label: Distance per day
exhibitNumbers.value: about 26 billion km a day (~173 times the Earth-Sun distance)

exhibitNumbers.label: Electrons in the ring
exhibitNumbers.value: 4.6 trillion (736 nanocoulombs)
exhibitNumbers.explanation: At 200 mA: charge = I / f0 = 0.2 A / 271,647 Hz = 736 nC = 4.6e12 electrons.

exhibitNumbers.label: Electrons in one bunch
exhibitNumbers.value: about 21 billion (216-bunch mode) up to 96 billion (48-bunch timing mode)
exhibitNumbers.explanation: 736 nC / 216 = 3.4 nC; 48-bunch mode 15.3 nC per bunch.
exhibitNumbers.source: derived; srp2024 Table 1 (9.6e10 electrons, 15.3 nC single bunch)

exhibitNumbers.label: Bunch spacing
exhibitNumbers.value: 17 ns apart in today's 216-bunch mode (a light-pulse every 17 billionths of a second); 77 ns in timing mode
exhibitNumbers.explanation: 1296 rf buckets / 216 = every 6th bucket x 2.84 ns, assuming the 216 bunches are evenly spaced (the fill-pattern spacing is not published); 1296 / 48 = every 27th bucket = 76.7 ns.

exhibitNumbers.label: Ring size
exhibitNumbers.value: 1,103.6 m around (~350 m across), 40 identical 27.6-m sectors

exhibitNumbers.label: A slightly smaller ring
exhibitNumbers.value: 38 cm shorter than the old ring
exhibitNumbers.explanation: New C 1103.608 m vs old 1103.986 m. The insertion-device straights were not allowed to move (so no ID beamline had to be realigned); keeping them fixed with the new arc geometry shortened the ring and moved the bending-magnet source points ~2-3 m upstream and ~40 mm inboard. The rf frequency went up by 341-342 ppm.

exhibitNumbers.label: Magnets
exhibitNumbers.value: 1,321 electromagnets (33 in each of the 40 sectors, plus one extra corrector near the injection point), of 15 main types, vs 1,097 in the old ring
exhibitNumbers.explanation: Per sector: 7 bending magnets, 6 reverse bends, 10 quadrupoles, 6 sextupoles and 4 fast correctors = 33; 33 x 40 + 1 = 1,321. Old ring: 80 dipoles, 400 quadrupoles, 280 sextupoles, 317 correctors, 20 skew quads.

exhibitNumbers.label: Bending magnets per sector
exhibitNumbers.value: 7 forward + 6 backward ('reverse') bends instead of 2
exhibitNumbers.explanation: Splitting each 9-degree arc over many gentle bends (plus a few small backward bends) keeps the electrons from spreading out.

exhibitNumbers.label: Total bending
exhibitNumbers.value: the beam is bent through 435 degrees per lap, not 360
exhibitNumbers.explanation: Forward bends total +397.8 deg, reverse bends -37.7 deg; net 360 deg.

exhibitNumbers.label: Magnet strength
exhibitNumbers.value: quadrupole gradients ~80-100 tesla per metre - about 4-5x the old ring's ~20 T/m
exhibitNumbers.explanation: Stronger focusing squeezes the beam; needs small 26-mm magnet bores and vanadium-permendur poles.

exhibitNumbers.label: Pre-built modules
exhibitNumbers.value: 200 modules, each up to ~6.5 m long and ~27 tonnes
exhibitNumbers.explanation: 5 modules per sector (DLM-A, QMQ-A, FODO, QMQ-B, DLM-B). Magnets were mounted and aligned on their plinths or girders in an off-site workspace before the shutdown, stored, then carried into the tunnel on 'Traksporters', placed within 25 mm, aligned to 1 mm and grouted to the floor.
exhibitNumbers.source: fdr2 2-3.4.2; fdr5 5-3; ipac21 ('pre-assembled (in an off-site workspace) and eventually moved into the ring tunnel using Traksporters'); desy24 slide 8; apsNSR

exhibitNumbers.label: Installation pace
exhibitNumbers.value: ~1.2 modules per day
exhibitNumbers.explanation: 200 modules between 2023-07-12 and 2023-12-20 (162 days).

exhibitNumbers.label: Alignment
exhibitNumbers.value: magnets on a module lined up to 15 micrometres rms (spec 30 um) - thinner than a human hair
exhibitNumbers.explanation: Measured after installation; module-to-module 50 um (x) and 35 um (y) rms vs +/-100 um spec, around a 1.1-km ring.

exhibitNumbers.label: Vibration budget
exhibitNumbers.value: quadrupoles may shake no more than 10 nanometres rms (1-100 Hz)
exhibitNumbers.explanation: Tolerance derived from the 10%-of-beam-size stability rule.

exhibitNumbers.label: Beam size at an undulator
exhibitNumbers.value: about 14 x 3 micrometres (flat mode) or 12 x 8 um (round mode), vs 275 x 10 um before
exhibitNumbers.explanation: Cross-section ~27-62 times smaller than the old beam (area ratio).

exhibitNumbers.label: Emittance
exhibitNumbers.value: ~42 pm natural vs 3,100 pm before - about 75 times smaller (APS rounds this to 'almost a factor of 100'); 28-44 pm measured depending on coupling
exhibitNumbers.explanation: Emittance = beam size x angular spread. 3,100 / 41.5 = 75. Measured: 44 pm horizontal (flat beam) or 28 pm horizontal / 31 pm vertical (round beam). The round beam's vertical emittance (31 pm) is only a little below the old ring's 40 pm, so in round mode almost all of the gain is horizontal.
exhibitNumbers.source: srp2024; ipac25 Table 1; fdr2 Table 2.1; sp2025
exhibitNumbers.note: Corrected by verifier: earlier text said the round-mode vertical emittance was 'not smaller than before'; 31 pm < 40 pm.

exhibitNumbers.label: Brightness
exhibitNumbers.value: up to 500 times brighter (x540 at 20 keV in the design)
exhibitNumbers.explanation: See brightness section.

exhibitNumbers.label: Vacuum chamber
exhibitNumbers.value: a 22-mm-wide tube (about the width of a coin) instead of a 42 x 85 mm chamber; ID chambers just 6.3 mm tall with 0.6-mm walls
exhibitNumbers.explanation: A tiny chamber lets magnet poles sit close to the beam for strong focusing.
exhibitNumbers.source: fdr2 2-3.1; fdr3 Table 3.27; pac95; apsNSR ('an inch or less wide')

exhibitNumbers.label: Power radiated by the beam
exhibitNumbers.value: ~0.59 MW from the bending magnets, up to ~0.9 MW with all undulators closed
exhibitNumbers.explanation: U0 = 2.935 MeV per turn (as-built model) x 0.2 A = 587 kW (FDR: 2.87 MeV -> 574 kW); maximum with IDs 4.47 MeV -> 894 kW; replaced each lap by 12 radio-frequency cavities.

exhibitNumbers.label: Energy stored in the beam
exhibitNumbers.value: 4.4 kilojoules - like a one-tonne car rolling at 3 m/s
exhibitNumbers.explanation: 6 GV x 736 nC = 4.42 kJ; 1/2 m v^2 with m = 1000 kg gives v = 2.97 m/s.

exhibitNumbers.label: Swap-out
exhibitNumbers.value: about every 20 seconds the weakest bunch (by then down to roughly half its starting charge) is kicked out to a dump and replaced in the same bucket by a fresh bunch of ~5-6 nC (~35 billion electrons) from the booster, using kicker pulses only ~11 ns long
exhibitNumbers.explanation: Kickers must hit one bunch and miss its neighbours 17 ns away in the 216-bunch fill (11.4 ns in the design 324-bunch mode). With 216 bunches each bunch is renewed about every 216 x 20 s = 72 minutes; with a ~2-h lifetime it loses ~45% of its charge in that time. BTS charge 5.4-6.1 nC for 17-23 s intervals (ler25 slide 23).
exhibitNumbers.note: Corrected by verifier: the earlier text said a whole ~5-nC bunch is 'thrown out'; ~5 nC is the injected (BTS) charge, while the outgoing bunch carries much less.

plainExplainers.whatIsSynchrotron: A synchrotron light source is a giant racetrack for electrons. The electrons are first accelerated in a straight 'linac', collected in a small ring, then sped up in a 'booster' ring until each one carries 6 billion electron-volts of energy - moving at 99.9999996% of the speed of light. They are then stored for hours in the main storage ring, a 1.1-km loop of magnets inside a vacuum pipe. Whenever a magnet bends their path, the electrons give off a flash of light in a narrow forward cone, like sparks flung off a spinning grinding wheel. For such fast electrons the light spans everything from infrared to hard X-rays, and the X-rays are what the APS is built for. Around the ring, 35 straight sections hold special magnet arrays (undulators) that make extra-bright X-ray beams, which travel down beamlines to experiment stations where scientists study everything from batteries to proteins. Radio-frequency cavities give back the energy the electrons lose as light on every lap.
plainExplainers.whatIsMBA: To go round a circle, the electrons must be bent through 360 degrees. In the old APS each of the 40 sectors bent the beam with just 2 big magnets, so every bend was fairly sharp - and each sharp bend shakes the electron cloud and makes it spread out. The upgrade uses a 'multi-bend achromat' (MBA): each sector now uses 7 gentler bends, with powerful focusing magnets in between that keep squeezing the beam. Theory says the beam's spread shrinks roughly with the cube of the number of bends, so going from 2 to 7 bends alone makes it about 40 times smaller. APS-U adds two clever tricks: bending magnets whose strength changes along their length, and six small 'reverse bends' per sector that bend the beam slightly the wrong way. The reverse bends give the designers an extra handle on how electrons of different energies are spread out inside the arc, which cut the design emittance from about 67 to 42 picometre-radians. Together with lowering the energy from 7 to 6 GeV, the beam's emittance dropped from about 3,100 to about 42 picometre-radians. 'Achromat' means electrons with slightly different energies all come out of the sector on the same path.
plainExplainers.whyEmittanceMatters: Emittance measures how big and how spread-out the electron beam is: its width multiplied by how much its electrons fan out in angle. X-rays inherit both. A beam that is wide and spreading is like a big floodlight; a tiny, parallel beam is like a laser pointer. Scientists want the laser pointer, because a tiny, parallel source can be focused to spots only nanometres across and stays bright far down a beamline. APS-U cut the horizontal emittance about 75-fold (3,100 to 42 picometre-radians), so the beam at an undulator went from about 275 x 10 micrometres to about 14 x 3 micrometres in the flat-beam mode (about 12 x 8 micrometres in the round-beam mode used for most user runs). Because the X-ray photons now come from a much smaller, better-aimed source, and the current is twice as high, the beam's brightness rises by up to 500 times.
plainExplainers.whatIsCoherence: Light is a wave. 'Coherent' light has wave crests that march in step, like soldiers in a parade, so it can make clean interference patterns - the way two pebbles dropped in a pond make a ripple pattern. A laser is highly coherent; a light bulb is not. An X-ray source is fully coherent only if its size times its angular spread is smaller than about the wavelength divided by 4 pi - about 10 picometre-radians for 10-keV X-rays. A larger source is only partly coherent, and only a small fraction of its photons can be used for coherent experiments: well under 0.1% of a 10-keV beam at the old APS, a few percent at APS-U, which together with better undulators and twice the current gives roughly 100 times more coherent photons. Coherent X-rays let scientists reconstruct images from interference ('speckle') patterns (ptychography, coherent diffraction imaging), with a resolution set by how far out the scattered signal can be recorded rather than by the quality of X-ray lenses, and watch how the speckle pattern flickers to measure how nanoparticles, polymer chains or magnetic domains move over time (X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy, XPCS).
plainExplainers.whatIsUndulator: An undulator is a row of magnets with alternating north and south poles - about 2.1-2.4 m long with a pattern repeating every 1.35 to 3.3 cm (one special electromagnetic undulator at sector 29 uses 12.5 cm). Electrons flying through it are wiggled gently left and right many times (about 60 to 175 periods). Because the electrons move at almost the speed of light, the light from each wiggle catches up and adds in step with the light from the others, so the X-rays come out as a very narrow, intense beam concentrated at particular colours (energies) and their harmonics. Opening or closing the gap between the top and bottom magnet rows (8.5 mm at closest for most devices, set with half-micrometre resolution) changes the field and tunes the X-ray energy. Superconducting undulators use coils of superconducting wire cooled to -269 C instead of permanent magnets, reaching stronger fields for very hard X-rays; eight were planned for APS-U but, as of September 2026, none is installed yet.
plainExplainers.whatIsSwapOut: In the old APS, electrons were 'topped up' by adding a small puff of new electrons to an existing bunch every minute or two - which needs a wide, gentle magnetic 'catch zone'. APS-U's strong focusing leaves almost no room for that (the stable region is only about +/-1.5 mm wide). So instead the APS swaps: a few hundred turns ahead of time a small 'decoherence' kick puffs up the weakest bunch so it cannot damage the dump; then three fast kickers, pulsing for only about 11 billionths of a second, knock that bunch out into a shielded dump and at the same instant place a brand-new, full bunch exactly into its place. APS-U was the first light source in the world to run this way.
plainExplainers.whatIsBunchLengthening: Electrons in a tightly packed bunch occasionally bump into each other and get knocked out of the beam (the Touschek effect), so small, dense bunches die quickly. APS-U uses a superconducting 'harmonic cavity' cooled to 2.1 K that the beam itself rings like a bell; its field stretches each bunch to 2-4 times its natural length, thinning the crowd and roughly doubling the beam lifetime without making the beam any wider.
plainExplainers.whyLowerEnergy: The upgrade lowered the electron energy from 7 to 6 GeV. Emittance grows with the square of energy, so 6 GeV gives a ~36% brightness gain; the magnets can be weaker for the same focusing; and the beam loses much less energy to radiation per lap (which scales with energy to the fourth power), which makes 200 mA - twice the old current - affordable in rf power. The trade-off is a beam that is more sensitive to collective instabilities and scattering.
plainExplainers.whyRoundBeams: APS-U usually runs with 'full coupling', sharing emittance about equally between horizontal and vertical (about 28-31 pm each) to make a nearly round beam. Spreading the electrons out vertically makes the bunches less dense, so fewer electrons are lost by bumping into each other (Touschek scattering) and the beam lasts longer; the design treated round beams as the default. A 'flat', low-coupling mode (about 40 x 4 pm) gives a much smaller vertical source and the highest brightness, at the cost of a shorter lifetime; it is workable for fills with many bunches.
plainExplainers.whyLowerEnergy_source: fdr2 2-1.3 (Choice of Beam Energy): emittance scales quadratically with energy (36% brightness gain), lower energy is more susceptible to wakefield instabilities, IBS and Touschek loss, magnet gradients scale with energy, and radiated power scales as E^4.
